newsitem.title: USA: House Republican lifts hold on antitrust nomination.
newsitem.headline: House Republican lifts hold on antitrust nomination.

text.p: Sen. Conrad Burns, a Montana Republican, said Wednesday he would no longer hold up a Senate vote on President Clinton's nomination of Joel Klein to head the Justice Department's antitrust division.

Burns had blocked the nomination because he thought Klein was dragging his heels on giving the Oklahoma phone company SBC, a large Bell operating system, more latitude to compete in the long-distance market.

But Burns changed his mind after meeting with Klein Wednesday and reading a detailed letter from Klein explaining his views on the long-distance market and the Justice Department investigation into Microsoft Corp.

"While I initially had concerns with some of this views, I believe they have been sufficiently addressed both in our meeting this evening and in his letter addressing my specific concerns," Burns said in a statement.

Klein has been serving as acting assistant attorney general for antitrust since the departure last year of Anne Bingaman. In that capacity, it has been his responsibility to carry out Congress's wishes -- expressed in a law passed last year -- to foster a competitive market in telecommunications.
Klein's nomination is still being held up by two lawmakers, including Sen. Ernest Hollings, a South Carolina Democrat and Sen. Ted Stevens, an Alaska Republican.

Hollings has put his own hold on the nomination, arguing the acting assistant attorney general had been too permissive with phone companies that want to merge, and a spokesman said he did not expect a reversal of that position soon.
"I don't see any rapid movement toward a successful conclusion," said Hollings' spokesman Maury Lane. He said no meetings were scheduled with Klein.

Klein was charged with the task of telling the Federal Communications Commission whether he believes local phone companies have permitted real local competition. Only once there is real local competition may local phone companies enter the long-distance market.
Last month Klein said that SBC could not enter the long distance market in Oklahoma because it had failed to foster long distance competition.
That angered Burns, who wanted it to be easier for SBC to sell long distance.

In his letter to Burns, Klein said the Justice Department standard was not "a metric test, and it does not require that a BOC lose any particular portion of market share before the Justice Department will support its entry into in-region long distance."
